name: Empiricism and the rejection of innate ideas
plain_explanation: Locke argued the mind starts as 'white paper, void of all characters' and that everything we know comes from experience -- either from the senses (sensation) or from noticing our own mental operations (reflection, or 'internal sense'). Nothing is built in beforehand.
precise_definition: The doctrine that all our knowledge (with the possible exception of logic and mathematics) is derived from experience; Book I of the Essay argues against Plato, Descartes, and the scholastics that there are no innate ideas or principles, and Book II shows in detail how experience generates our various ideas.
why_it_mattered: Russell calls this Locke's 'bold innovation': in Locke's day the mind was widely supposed to know things a priori, so the complete dependence of knowledge on perception was revolutionary, even though it later became part of educated common sense in English-speaking countries.
historical_origin: Developed across Books I and II of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), directly opposing the rationalism of Descartes and Leibniz and the scholastic tradition Locke encountered at Oxford.
examples: The 'white paper' (tabula rasa) image for the mind before experience
Locke's two sources of ideas: sensation and reflection on 'the operation of our own mind'
competing_positions: Descartes' and Leibniz's belief in innate ideas and a priori metaphysical knowledge
Plato's Theaetetus, which had argued against identifying knowledge with perception
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became the foundation stone of the British empiricist tradition running through Berkeley and Hume to J. S. Mill.
